entry: Region and former province on the western coast of the [[Netherlands]]. As a county, it was a unified political region within the Holy Roman Empire from the 10th to the 16th century. In the 17th century the province dominated the other provinces of the Dutch Republic as a maritime and economic power. The former county roughly coincides with the current provinces of North Holland and South Holland. These provinces include the capital, [[Amsterdam]], the home of Europe's largest port, [[Rotterdam]], and the seat of government, [[The Hague]]. In 2019 the Netherlands officially dropped its support for using Holland for the whole country.

American actress. Born in Conyers, Georgia, she graduated in drama from Carnegie Mellon University in [[Pittsburgh]]. After starring in *Broadcast News* (1987), she received her first [[Academy Awards]] nomination. She won two Primetime Emmy Awards for lead actress in the television films *Roe vs. Wade* (1989) and *The Positively True Adventures of the Alleged Texas Cheerleader-Murdering Mom* (1993). She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *The Piano* (1993) and was nominated for Best Supporting Actress for *The Firm* (1993). Other major accolades include an AACTA Award, a BAFTA Award, a Cannes Film Festival Award and a Golden Globe.

Neighborhood in central [[Los Angeles]], [[California]]. Its name has become synonymous with the American film industry, and it is sometimes informally called Tinseltown. Most major film studios are located outside the neighborhood, although [[Paramount Pictures]] maintains a studio lot within it. The name came from an estate in [[Illinois]] and was adopted for a land subdivision in August 1887. Hollywood was incorporated as an independent municipality on November 9, 1903, and consolidated with Los Angeles on February 7, 1910, following a referendum.

Sidewalk landmark in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]]. The Walk of Fame has more than 2,800 five-pointed terrazzo-and-brass stars set into sidewalks along Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street. Each star honors achievement in entertainment, and names include actors, filmmakers and musicians. The walk was conceived in 1953, the first stars were unveiled in 1958, and the first permanent stars were placed in 1960. The Hollywood Chamber of Commerce administers it, and sponsors pay fees to fund each star. It received an estimated ten million visitors a year in 2010, and is one of Los Angeles's most popular tourist attractions.

Chemical element with symbol Ho and atomic number 67. A rare-earth element and the eleventh member of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series, holmium is a relatively soft, silvery, malleable metal that is fairly corrosion-resistant. It is too reactive to occur in native form, and pure holmium slowly forms a yellowish oxide coating in air. Swedish chemist Per Theodor Cleve isolated it, while Jacques-Louis Soret and Marc Delafontaine observed it spectroscopically in 1878. The name comes from Holmia, the Latin name for [[Stockholm]]. Holmium has the highest magnetic permeability and magnetic saturation of any element, so it is used in the pole pieces of the strongest static [[Magnet|magnets]]. It strongly absorbs [[Neutron|neutrons]] and serves as a burnable poison in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]].

Current geological epoch, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago. It follows the [[Last Glacial Period]] and, with the preceding [[Pleistocene]], forms the [[Quaternary]] period. The Holocene is an interglacial period equivalent to Marine Isotope Stage 1. Because it corresponds with the rapid growth and impact of the human species, it is often called the Age of Humans. Its ecosystems continue to be affected by the [[Holocene extinction]], largely of human causation. In July 2018 the International Union of Geological Sciences divided the epoch into three ages: the Greenlandian (11,700 to 8,200 years ago), the Northgrippian (8,200 to 4,200 years ago) and the Meghalayan (4,200 years ago to the present).

Ongoing extinction event caused by human activity. It affects many families of plants and animals, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish and invertebrates. It is sometimes called the sixth extinction. Estimated extinction rates are 100 to 1,000 times higher than natural background rates, though a higher estimate of 10,000 times remains controversial. Drivers include [[Climate change|climate change]], wetland destruction, [[Deforestation|deforestation]], overfishing, ocean acidification, population and economic growth, and [[Pollution|pollution]]. A 1998 survey by the [[American Museum of Natural History]] found that 70% of biologists acknowledged an ongoing anthropogenic extinction event.

[[Famine|Man-made famine]] in Soviet Ukraine, 1932–1933. It killed millions of Ukrainians and was part of a wider Soviet famine of 1930–1933 that affected the major grain-producing areas of the [[Soviet Union]]. Scholars agree that the famine was primarily man-made, but it remains disputed whether it was intentional, directed at Ukrainians or constitutes a [[Genocide|genocide]]. Some historians conclude that [[Joseph Stalin]] deliberately engineered it to eliminate a Ukrainian independence movement, while others attribute it mainly to collectivization and industrialization. A joint statement to the [[United Nations]] signed by 25 countries in November 2003 put the death toll at 7 to 10 million, while more recent scholarship estimates between 3.5 and 5 million. Public discussion was banned in the Soviet Union until the glasnost reforms of [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] in the 1980s. Since 2006 Ukraine, 33 other UN member states, the [[European Parliament]] and 35 of the 50 U.S. states have recognized it as a genocide.

Imaging technique for recording and reconstructing a wavefront. A hologram records an interference pattern made by overlaying a reference beam onto the wavefront of interest. When suitably lit, it diffracts light to reproduce the original light field, including depth cues such as [[Parallax|parallax]]. The technique is best known for three-dimensional images but is also used in data storage, [[Interferometry|interferometry]] and microscopy. Hungarian-British physicist Dennis Gabor invented holography in 1948 while seeking to improve image resolution in [[Electron microscope|electron microscopes]]. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1971. Optical holography did not advance until the [[Laser|laser]] was developed in 1960. Mass-produced, low-cost laser diodes, such as those in [[DVD]] recorders, have made holography more accessible to researchers, artists and hobbyists.

Complex-valued function of one or more complex variables, complex differentiable in a neighborhood of each point of a domain. Such a function is infinitely differentiable and locally equal to its own [[Taylor series]]. Holomorphic functions are the central objects of study in [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]]. Analytic function is often used as a synonym, and a major theorem shows that holomorphic functions are complex analytic, and vice versa. A holomorphic function whose domain is the whole complex plane is called an entire function. A holomorphic function has real and imaginary parts u and v that satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations. Complex differentiability is a stronger condition than real differentiability.

International breed or group of breeds of dairy cattle. In modern US English, Holstein refers to animals based almost exclusively on stock from the Netherlands. The breeds are considered separate in the [[United Kingdom|UK]], but they are so similar that they cannot be distinguished for statistical purposes; Friesian is the more common term there. An average US Holstein cow produces about 22,000 pounds (10,000 kg) of milk per year. European Holsteins average 7,000 to 8,000 [[Litre|liters]] a year, a difference attributed to the American use of hormones, which is outlawed in Europe. Lifetime yield averages around 30,000 liters regardless of country. The breed has one of the largest gene pools in the world, and the bull Round Oak Rag Apple Elevation fathered over 70,000 offspring through artificial insemination. Cross-breeding is popular in some countries, such as [[New Zealand]], to gain hybrid vigor.

Treasure motif in Arthurian literature. Various traditions describe it as a cup, dish or stone with miraculous healing powers, often guarded by the Fisher King in a hidden Grail castle. A mysterious grail first appears in *Perceval, the Story of the Grail*, an unfinished chivalric romance by [[Chrétien de Troyes]] written around 1190. Shortly afterward, Robert de Boron portrayed it as the vessel of the Last Supper, which Joseph of Arimathea used to catch the blood of [[Jesus]]. Wolfram von Eschenbach described it as a stone in *Parzival*. The Grail was later linked to the Holy Chalice in the Lancelot-Grail cycle and the 15th-century *Le Morte d'Arthur*. Its origins, whether Christian, Celtic or other, remain uncertain and debated. Today the Grail is a popular theme in culture, and by analogy any elusive goal may be called a holy grail.

Central governing body of the [[Catholic Church]] and [[Vatican City]]. According to Catholic tradition it was founded in the first century by [[Saint Peter]] and Saint Paul. It encompasses the office of the [[Pope|pope]], as bishop of Rome, and is administered through the Roman Curia. Under international law the Holy See holds the status of a sovereign juridical entity. Vatican City was established by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, agreed with the Kingdom of Italy, to ensure the independence of the papacy. The Holy See maintains bilateral diplomatic relations with 180 sovereign states and engages in multilateral diplomacy with the [[United Nations]] and the [[European Union]]. Papal nuncios represent the Holy See, not Vatican City State.

Concept within [[Abrahamic religions]], also known as the Holy Ghost. In Judaism it is the divine quality or force of God manifesting in the world, particularly in prophecy, creation and guidance. In Nicene Christianity it is the third person of the [[Trinity]], co-equal and co-eternal with God the Father and God the Son. In Islam it acts as an agent of divine communication and typically refers to the angel [[Gabriel]], who brings revelation. In the Bahá'í Faith it is the intermediary between God and man. In Christian iconography, the Holy Spirit is shown as a winged dove or tongues of fire, drawn from New Testament accounts of the baptism of [[Jesus]] in the [[Jordan River]] and the day of Pentecost.

1990 American Christmas comedy film directed by Chris Columbus. Written and produced by [[John Hughes]], it stars Macaulay Culkin as Kevin McCallister, an eight-year-old who defends his suburban [[Chicago]] home from two burglars after his family accidentally leaves him behind on a Christmas trip to [[Paris]]. Filming took place on location across [[Illinois]]. The film grossed $476.7 million worldwide, becoming the second-highest-grossing film of 1990, and it was nominated for two [[Academy Awards]]. In 2023 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry, and five sequels have followed.

American multinational home improvement retail corporation. It sells tools, construction products, building materials, appliances and services, and is the largest home improvement specialty retailer in the [[United States]]. In fiscal 2024 the company reported $159.5 billion in revenue and approximately 470,100 associates. Co-founded in 1978, it opened its first two stores in metro [[Atlanta]] in 1979. Its big-box stores operate across the United States, in all 10 provinces of [[Canada]], and in all 31 Mexican states and Mexico City. Headquartered in Cobb County, Georgia, it has been listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] since 1984.

Machine for household tasks such as [[Cooking|cooking]], cleaning and [[Food preservation|food preservation]]. The self-contained electric and gas-powered appliances were a uniquely American innovation of the early 20th century, tied to the decline of full-time domestic servants and the desire to reduce household chores. Early examples included washing machines, water heaters, refrigerators and sewing machines. Dishwashers and clothes dryers spread after World War II. The National Appliance Energy Conservation Act of 1987 mandated a 25% reduction in energy consumption every five years. By the 1990s five companies sold over 90% of products. Major appliances, or white goods, include refrigerators and washing machines, small appliances include toasters, and [[Consumer electronics|consumer electronics]], or brown goods, include TVs and computers.

Process of renovating, improving or adding to a home. Projects may upgrade the interior, such as [[Plumbing|plumbing]] and electrical systems, or the exterior, such as [[Masonry|masonry]], [[Concrete|concrete]], siding and roofing. Common goals are comfort, maintenance and repair, additional living space, saving energy, and safety or privacy. Energy-saving measures include insulation, replacement [[Window|windows]], lighting, solar panels, [[Wind turbine|wind turbines]] and geothermal heat pumps. Safety upgrades may include fire sprinkler systems, smoke detectors and technical protection against [[Natural disaster|natural disasters]].

Condition of lacking stable, safe and adequate housing. Definitions vary by country, but a 2009 United Nations census guideline distinguishes primary homelessness, living on the streets without shelter, from secondary homelessness, moving between temporary shelters such as the houses of friends and family, [[Hotel|hotels]] and emergency accommodation. Homelessness and [[Poverty|poverty]] are closely interrelated. There is no standardized method for counting homeless people, so most cities have only estimated figures. In 2025 approximately 330 million people worldwide experienced absolute homelessness, lacking any form of shelter. Article 25 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]], adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 1948, recognizes the right to a standard of living adequate for health and well-being, including housing.

Pseudoscientific system of [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]], conceived in 1796 by German physician Samuel Hahnemann. Its practitioners believe that a substance causing symptoms in healthy people can cure similar symptoms in the sick. Remedies are diluted repeatedly, often until not a single molecule of the original substance remains. Clinical trials have generally demonstrated no objective effect from its preparations. It was introduced to the [[United States]] in 1825. It revived in the 1970s alongside the [[New Age]] movement. The scientific and medical communities have characterized it as [[Quackery|quackery]] and [[Fraud|fraud]]. Meta-analyses in the 21st century have shown its therapeutic claims lack scientific justification.

Tasks assigned to students by teachers to be completed at home. Common assignments include required reading, writing projects, math problems and review before tests. Its effects are debated. Homework has not been shown to improve academic performance among young children, though proponents claim it builds good study habits. Among teenagers, more homework generally goes with higher grades, but large amounts of homework worsen performance, even among older students. Students who have more than 90 minutes of homework a day in middle school, or more than two hours in high school, score worse on standardized tests. Low-achieving students benefit more, yet teachers commonly assign them less homework. Homework also causes stress for students and parents and reduces time for other activities.

Family of primates, whose members are known as the great apes. It includes eight extant species in four genera: *Pongo* (orangutans), *Gorilla* (gorillas), *Pan* (chimpanzees and [[Bonobo|bonobos]]) and *Homo*, of which only modern humans remain. The most recent common ancestor of the family lived roughly 14 million years ago. Because humans and the other great apes are closely related, some [[Animal rights|animal rights]] organizations argue that nonhuman great apes deserve basic human rights. 29 countries have instituted research bans to protect great apes from any kind of scientific testing.

Subfamily of [[Hominidae]] that includes humans, chimpanzees and gorillas, also called African hominids or African apes. It has two tribes, Hominini and Gorillini. Hominini comprises the genus [[Homo]], with modern humans and many extinct species, and the genus *Pan*, which includes chimpanzees and bonobos. Gorillini contains the genus *Gorilla*. The subfamily comprises all hominids that arose after orangutans (Ponginae) split from the great ape line. Traces of extinct Homo species, including [[Homo floresiensis]], have been found with dates as recent as 40,000 years ago. Until 1970 the family Hominidae meant humans only, and by 1990 gorillas and chimpanzees were also placed in Homininae.

Tribe of the subfamily [[Homininae]], comprising the genera [[Homo]] and *Pan*. The term was introduced by Camille Arambourg in 1948. Traditionally, chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans were grouped as pongids, but genetic evidence shows that humans, chimpanzees and gorillas are more closely related to each other than to orangutans. Gorillas are placed in the separate tribe Gorillini, and usage remains contested: some exclude *Pan* from Hominini. Subtribe Hominina includes humans and many extinct relatives, while subtribe Panina contains chimpanzees and bonobos.

Genus of great apes, with a single living species, *Homo sapiens*. The name derives from the Latin *homo*, meaning human being. The oldest member is [[Homo habilis]], known from fossils just over 2 million years old. [[Homo erectus]] appeared about 2 million years ago and spread through Africa and Eurasia in several migrations. Anatomically modern humans emerged in Africa close to 300,000 to 200,000 years ago, while *H. neanderthalensis* emerged around the same time in Europe and western Asia. [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] are thought to have survived until around 40,000 years ago. Its closest living relatives are the [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzees]] and bonobos of the genus *Pan*, from which the lineages diverged 5.7–11 million years ago.
